Inside the ML Layer · Part 3 · Parallelism

Splitting the Giant: The Libraries That Spread One Model Across 16,000 GPUs

No frontier model fits on one chip. Between the framework (Part 2) and the kernels (Part 4) sits a layer of libraries whose only job is to split a model, its data and its optimizer across thousands of GPUs while keeping them busy: NVIDIA's Megatron-Core, Microsoft's DeepSpeed, PyTorch's FSDP2 and TorchTitan, Google's MaxText, and DeepSeek's in-house stack. This part explains what each one does, why pipelines leave GPUs idle, why mixture-of-experts models need their own tricks, and how to choose.

3. Five ways to split a model

Every library combines the same five ideas. Producing Intelligence Part 4 follows them through Meta's Llama 3 run; here is the short version, with what each one costs.

1. Data parallel (DP) + shardingEach group of GPUs sees different data. Plain DP copies the whole model to every GPU; ZeRO and FSDP shard optimizer state (stage 1), gradients (stage 2) and weights (stage 3) across them, gathering weights just in time.Cost: all-gather and reduce-scatter every layer; works across slower links.
2. Tensor parallel (TP)Each layer's big matrices are cut into slices on different GPUs, which compute partial results and combine them. Megatron-LM's 2019 design for transformer layers is still the standard.Cost: several all-reduces per layer; needs NVLink, so usually ≤ 8 GPUs (one server) or one NVL72 rack.
3. Pipeline parallel (PP)Consecutive layers live on different GPUs; micro-batches flow through like an assembly line.Cost: idle "bubbles" at the start and end of each step (section 7); little communication.
4. Context / sequence parallel (CP)A very long sequence is split along its length; attention needs keys and values from other chunks, passed in a ring or swapped all-to-all.Cost: extra attention communication; essential above ~32K tokens.
5. Expert parallel (EP)In mixture-of-experts models, different experts live on different GPUs and tokens are sent to whichever experts the router chooses.Cost: two all-to-alls per MoE layer, often across nodes.

5. The libraries

Two families have emerged. Megatron-style libraries hand-engineer each transformer block for tensor and pipeline parallelism and squeeze out the last few percent on NVIDIA hardware. Sharding-first designs (FSDP2, TorchTitan, JAX with XLA) treat parallelism as a layout of arrays on a device mesh and compose the dimensions more freely. In 2026 they borrow from each other constantly: TorchTitan adds pipeline schedules and Float8, Megatron-Core adds FSDP, and both import ideas DeepSeek open-sourced.

7. The bubble problem

Pipelines have a structural flaw: the last stage cannot start until the first has finished, and the first sits idle while the last finishes the backward pass. That idle time is the bubble. With p stages and m micro-batches, GPipe's bubble fraction is (p − 1) / (m + p − 1). More micro-batches shrink it, but each one needs stored activations.

Pipeline schedule animator

4 stages. Forward = 1 time unit, backward = 2. Grey = idle. Our own simulation of the textbook schedules.

ForwardBackwardIdle (bubble)
2018GPipeAll forwards, then all backwards. Simple; stores activations for all m micro-batches.
2019–211F1B (PipeDream)Same bubble, but alternates forward and backward so each stage holds at most p micro-batches of activations.
2021Interleaved 1F1BMegatron gives each GPU several smaller chunks of layers (v), cutting the bubble roughly v-fold at the cost of more communication.
2023Zero bubbleSplits backward into input-gradient and weight-gradient work and schedules weight gradients into the gaps.
2024DualPipeDeepSeek feeds micro-batches from both ends and overlaps computation with communication; fewer bubbles than prior methods, per the V3 report.

8. Mixture of experts makes it harder

Tokens on the move

Each token is routed to a few experts that may live on other GPUs: one all-to-all to send it, another to bring the result back. Tap Route.

Mixture-of-experts models such as DeepSeek-V3 activate only a fraction of their parameters per token, which makes them cheap to train for their size but heavy on communication: every MoE layer needs two all-to-all exchanges, often across InfiniBand between servers. The DeepSeek-V3 report describes custom cross-node all-to-all kernels that use both InfiniBand and NVLink while tying up few streaming multiprocessors, and DualPipe to hide that communication behind computation. DeepSeek later open-sourced these pieces (DeepEP for expert-parallel communication and DualPipe), and they have since been integrated into other stacks. If the router sends too many tokens to one expert, that GPU becomes the bottleneck: load balancing is a parallelism problem as much as a modelling one.

9. Long context

Ring attention / context parallelThe sequence is cut into chunks; each GPU keeps its queries and passes keys and values around a ring so every chunk attends to every other. Meta used context parallelism to extend Llama 3 to 128K tokens; TorchTitan's tables show Llama 3.1 405B trained up to 262,144 tokens with CP 8 (at 16 tokens per second per GPU, against 76 at 32K).
DeepSpeed-UlyssesInstead of a ring, an all-to-all swaps the split from sequence to attention heads, so each GPU computes full attention for a subset of heads, then swaps back. Limited by the number of heads, but simple and fast on good networks.

11. Reported performance

What the papers say

Each bar is a different kind of number from a different setup. Read the label, not the length.

MFU = model FLOPs utilisation, the share of the chips' peak compute spent on the model's maths. Llama 3: BF16 MFU 38–43% on 8K–16K H100s (Meta). Megatron 2021: 52% of peak on 3,072 A100s for a 1T-parameter model (Narayanan et al.). TorchTitan: speedups over its own optimised baselines on H100s.

12. Choosing a library

Which library fits?

An editorial guide.

VerdictParallelism libraries are where a lab's scale is won or lost. For dense models on NVIDIA GPUs, Megatron-Core remains the performance benchmark, while FSDP2 and TorchTitan offer a simpler, PyTorch-native path that has closed much of the gap. For mixture-of-experts models, DeepSeek's open-sourced communication tools changed what everyone else considers possible. On TPUs, JAX and XLA do most of this for you. The largest labs still build their own; what they publish suggests the ideas are now shared and the advantage lies in engineering and hardware co-design.

13. Reading the numbers

Primary
Llama 3: 16,384 H100s, 38–43% MFU, 4D parallelism, 128K context with CP (Meta paper). DeepSeek-V3: 2,048 H800s, HAI-LLM, DualPipe, custom all-to-all kernels, 2.788M H800 GPU-hours (report). TorchTitan: +65.08% (8B, 128 GPUs), +12.59% (70B, 256 GPUs), +30% (405B, 512 GPUs) over optimised baselines; 405B throughput 76 → 16 tokens/s/GPU from 32K to 262K context (paper). Megatron-Core announced Jan 2024 (NVIDIA repository). DeepSpeed accepted as a PyTorch Foundation hosted project, May 2025, after Microsoft contributed it to the Linux Foundation (PyTorch Foundation).
Formulas
GPipe and 1F1B bubble: (p − 1)/(m + p − 1). Interleaved schedules reduce it roughly by the number of chunks per GPU.
